title: David Baggett vs Matt Dillahunty: The Moral Argument for God
label: Moral authority, God, and secular ethics
motion: Do objective moral facts, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and moral rationality make theism a better explanation than secular ethical theories?

sections.title: Abductive Method, Candidate Pool, and Conclusion

pro.words: Compare theistic and secular ethical theories by their explanatory treatment of moral facts, moral knowledge, transformation, and moral rationality.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The framework clearly integrates four independently significant moral phenomena, identifies theistic and secular candidates, and adopts comparative explanatory criteria while preserving an explicitly limited evidential purpose. Principal limitation: Establishing a well-organized comparison does not independently demonstrate that every listed phenomenon requires further explanation or that the proposed candidates possess sufficiently discriminating explanatory content. Live burden: The account must justify explanandum status, specify candidate eligibility, and show comparative advantage against developed secular alternatives rather than relying primarily upon the phenomena's intuitive seriousness. Locked score: The very strong band appropriately reflects exceptional motion-level relevance, recoverable structure, careful qualification, and substantial coherence, while retaining measured reservations about evidential establishment and candidate specification.

con.words: The abductive case must justify both the asserted moral explananda and God’s eligibility as a reasonable explanatory candidate before comparison can support theism.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The objection directly identifies two indispensable prerequisites for Baggett's abduction, distinguishing whether the moral phenomena need explanation from whether God qualifies as a sufficiently specified candidate. Principal limitation: It moves somewhat quickly from missing justification within the presentation to broader explanatory inadequacy, although a comparative hypothesis can initially enter consideration before receiving complete confirmation. Live burden: Dillahunty must explain the appropriate candidacy threshold without demanding deductive demonstration, while Baggett must supply positive reasons for both explanandum status and meaningful theistic specification. Locked score: The very strong band reflects precise motion-level contact, excellent diagnostic responsiveness, stable conditional structure, and appropriately charitable engagement, with modest evidential restraint warranted by the objection's accelerated inference.

pro.words: Even comparative explanatory success yields only some reason for theism within total evidence and cannot overcome sufficiently unfavorable prior considerations.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett sharply limits the inference to contributory moral evidence, explicitly allowing that the total evidential record could still favor atheism despite local comparative success for theism. Principal limitation: Narrowing the conclusion does not itself establish positive likelihood value, answer the candidacy objection, or show that secular mechanisms fail across the proposed moral phenomena. Live burden: The affirmative must demonstrate an actual comparative increment after accounting for prior plausibility, candidate-pool incompleteness, combined alternatives, and the unresolved distinction between ordinary and complete transformation. Locked score: The very strong band reflects exceptional calibration, inferential clarity, representational charity, and central relevance, while recognizing that qualification responsibly bounds rather than independently validates the abductive case.

con.words: Abductive confidence must be proportioned to the quality, representativeness, and depth of the available pool of candidate explanations.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The methodological constraint directly addresses comparative confidence, explaining why the best option within a shallow or unrepresentative candidate pool may remain far from a reasonable conclusion. Principal limitation: The move does not inventory specific omitted candidates or demonstrate that the present pool is materially defective, while Baggett already limits his conclusion to some evidential reason. Live burden: Dillahunty must connect general bad-lot risk to this comparison, and Baggett must establish that the relevant secular combinations and theistic alternatives are representative enough for positive support. Locked score: The very strong band reflects exceptionally clear conditional reasoning, strong responsiveness, careful uncertainty, and important methodological relevance, while preserving a modest limitation concerning debate-specific evidential application.

sections.title: Objective Moral Facts and Categorical Authority

pro.words: Objective values concern intrinsic moral goodness, whereas objective duties are binding, prescriptive, authoritative requirements that are at least sometimes categorical.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The definition carefully distinguishes evaluative goodness from deontic obligation and preserves the important qualification that categorical, exceptionless force belongs to at least some duties rather than all. Principal limitation: Terminological clarity cannot independently establish that such duties exist, possess irreducible authority, or require the personal explanatory ground subsequently proposed by the affirmative. Live burden: Baggett must move from stipulated categories to defensible moral phenomena and then demonstrate why instrumental, contractual, naturalistic, or axiomatic accounts cannot adequately accommodate their apparent authority. Locked score: The very strong band reflects outstanding precision, coherence, calibration, and central relevance to the moral explananda, while retaining an evidential reservation appropriate to a definition rather than an existence argument.

con.words: Variable guilt cannot establish objective morality, while consequences can be assessed objectively relative to adopted goals such as survival and well-being.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty distinguishes subjective adoption of a goal from objective assessment of consequences, while cultural variability provides a relevant caution against treating guilt as an infallible moral detector. Principal limitation: Well-being remains expressly broad and ill-defined, and goal-relative objectivity does not fully answer Baggett's claim that some obligations bind categorically regardless of an agent's adopted ends. Live burden: The secular account must specify well-being, explain difficult tradeoffs, and preserve the narrower possibility that some guilt experiences defeasibly track wrongdoing despite considerable cultural distortion. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects substantial coherence, careful boundedness, and direct relevance, while registering incomplete contact with categorical authority and limited development of the proposed evaluative standard.

pro.words: A loving creator who enables moral apprehension offers an explanation for binding, objective, prescriptive obligations, provided that such authority is real.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett connects the disputed phenomenology of binding obligation to a personal explanatory candidate and expressly acknowledges that an adequate denial of additional authority would block this proposal. Principal limitation: The presentation does not derive authority from loving creation or sufficiently compare the hypothesis with secular, nonpersonal, axiomatic, and constitutivist alternatives possessing different theoretical commitments. Live burden: The affirmative must first establish irreducibly categorical authority, then explain how a creator grounds rather than merely endorses obligation and how human apprehension reliably accesses that authority. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects direct comparative relevance, meaningful concession, and a recoverable explanatory proposal, while appropriately registering limited warrant, implicit conditionality, and insufficiently developed comparative advantage.

con.words: After concern for well-being is adopted, actions can be evaluated by whether they advance that goal without adding further categorical oughts.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty candidly identifies concern for well-being as the nonderived commitment and clearly separates that initial normative adoption from subsequent factual assessment of goal-directed consequences. Principal limitation: Saying no further oughts remain overstates what has been shown because measurement standards, interpersonal tradeoffs, uncertainty, and conflicts among dimensions of well-being can introduce additional normative choices. Live burden: The account must justify or appropriately bound the initial commitment and explain why conditional evaluation adequately answers purported obligations binding agents who reject, misunderstand, or narrowly construe well-being. Locked score: The very strong band reflects intellectual correction, transparent conditional structure, strong responsiveness, and central secular relevance, while preserving reservations about categorical authority and hidden normativity within implementation.

pro.words: Guilt’s experienced authority can provide defeasible evidence of genuine wrongdoing and need not be explained exhaustively as cultural conditioning.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett carefully presents guilt as potential evidence rather than an infallible foundation, preserving a modest phenomenological claim while expressly denying that the entire argument depends upon it. Principal limitation: The support remains substantially introspective, and authoritative feeling can arise through cultural formation, psychological mechanisms, or mistaken conscience without reliably tracking objective moral truth. Live burden: The affirmative must identify reliability conditions, distinguish veridical from distorted guilt, and explain what the phenomenology contributes beyond evidence already supplied by independently accepted moral judgments. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects commendable qualification, relevance, and preservation of the secular alternative, while appropriately limiting credit for evidential warrant and generalization from personal experience.

con.words: Empathy, universalization, and role reversal can explain conscience and much apparent authority without religious commands or another supernatural foundation.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply offers an intelligible psychological account of conscience through empathy and perspective-taking while avoiding the simplistic claim that moral experience merely repeats parental, communal, or religious instruction. Principal limitation: A causal explanation of why demands feel authoritative does not yet establish their truth, categorical force, or capacity to override self-interest when empathy becomes partial or absent. Live burden: Dillahunty must bridge motivational psychology and normative justification, explaining how role reversal supports reliable principles while accommodating conflicts among persons, interests, animals, and long-term consequences. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects coherent secular explanatory contact, stable scope, and charitable engagement, while preserving a substantial unresolved bridge from empathic origins to objective authority.

pro.words: Exceptionally obvious foundational moral principles may rationally function as properly basic axioms from which further ethical conclusions are inferred.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The proposal explains why ethical reasoning may legitimately begin from exceptionally obvious principles when no more evident supporting premise is available, without pretending every intuition receives foundational status. Principal limitation: Proper basicality can provide prima facie rational permission without independently establishing reliability, objective truth, or the distinctively theistic origin required by the broader comparative argument. Live burden: Baggett must specify defeaters, manage disagreement, and distinguish truth-tracking moral apprehension from convergence produced by shared cognition, social learning, empathy, or evolutionary pressures. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects a carefully restricted epistemological reframe, strong coherence, and meaningful relevance, while appropriately reserving judgment about reliability and the additional inference from basic knowledge to theism.

con.words: Divine grounding cannot resolve practical moral disagreement unless people can reliably identify the good deity and access that deity’s requirements.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The objection separates moral ontology from epistemic and practical payoff, using persistent religious disagreement to show that divine grounding alone does not reliably resolve contested requirements. Principal limitation: Imperfect identification does not refute the existence of objective morality or its possible divine foundation, so the challenge primarily weakens explanatory advantage concerning knowledge and application. Live burden: Baggett must explain noncircular identification, error correction, and accessible moral guidance, while Dillahunty must avoid treating fallible access as evidence against every possible underlying moral reality. Locked score: The very strong band reflects exceptional directness, stable scope, strong historical motivation, and precise contact with the moral-knowledge burden, while preserving the important distinction between epistemic limitation and ontological refutation.

pro.words: The distinctive issue is whether secular naturalism can sustain realistic hope for complete moral transformation, not whether ordinary improvement plainly occurs.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The move charitably concedes ordinary secular improvement and isolates a more ambitious transformative horizon, thereby preventing observable behavioral progress from automatically exhausting the affirmative's intended explanandum. Principal limitation: Complete moral transformation receives no sufficiently precise success condition, and the presentation offers limited support that such hope is realistic, widespread, or independently explanation-demanding. Live burden: Baggett must define completeness, establish why aspiration constitutes evidence about reality, and explain why attainable secular formation is insufficient for the motion's transformation component. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects a clear conceptual distinction, explicit qualification, and constructive comparative relevance, while appropriately registering substantial uncertainty about specification, evidential warrant, and explanatory necessity.

con.words: Ordinary moral improvement can arise through secular natural processes, while even false beliefs about divine supervision may motivate beneficial behavior.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The reply supplies a concrete secular alternative for moral change and usefully separates a belief's behavioral effectiveness from its truth, directly undercutting distinctively theistic explanatory necessity. Principal limitation: Its examples principally concern ordinary behavioral improvement, whereas Baggett's later formulation concerns realistic hope for complete transformation, a substantially broader and more demanding prospective horizon. Live burden: The secular account must clarify whether the motion requires explaining observable improvement, aspirational perfection, or both, and identify mechanisms proportionate to whichever transformation concept remains relevant. Locked score: The very strong band reflects direct comparative contact, careful possibility-level calibration, and coherent causal reasoning, while preserving reservations about evidential development and incomplete engagement with total transformation.

pro.words: Some obligations bind categorically and therefore cannot be reduced to instrumental reasoning about achieving goals an agent has already adopted.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett grants the legitimacy of goal-directed practical reasoning and then precisely isolates the remaining issue: whether at least some moral obligations bind independently of an agent's chosen ends. Principal limitation: The distinction identifies what instrumental accounts leave unexplained only if categorical obligations genuinely exist, so the move still depends upon contested phenomenology and foundational moral judgment. Live burden: The affirmative must defend categorical authority without stipulation, while the secular side must explain agents who reject well-being yet appear obligated by duties concerning cruelty, justice, and impartiality. Locked score: The very strong band reflects excellent diagnostic contact, disciplined qualification, conceptual clarity, and central relevance, while retaining an evidential reservation about the existence and scope of categorical requirements.

con.words: Shared creaturely needs can support convergence on human-benefiting axioms that generate coherent ethical systems under entirely godless physical conditions.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty accepts foundational starting points and offers shared physical needs as a plausible secular explanation for convergence on principles favoring life, health, and reduced suffering. Principal limitation: The random-selection illustration obscures justificatory standards, while coherent system construction and practical convergence do not alone establish objective truth, categorical authority, or dependable handling of conflicts. Live burden: The account must explain why particular axioms deserve endorsement, how revisions occur, and whether common human interests reliably extend toward outsiders, animals, future persons, and costly impartial duties. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects direct comparative engagement, possibility-level calibration, and useful explanatory economy, while preserving important reservations concerning epistemic warrant, normative authority, and underspecified convergence.

pro.words: A human-flourishing account may be too narrow because animal suffering and moral character can matter beyond immediate human benefit.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: The cat-torture example provides a vivid and specific scope test, while attention to the wrongdoer's character adds a distinct evaluative dimension beyond immediate consequences for human flourishing. Principal limitation: A sufficiently inclusive well-being framework can incorporate animal welfare, ecological interests, and character effects, so the example challenges the presented specification more clearly than the framework's viability. Live burden: Dillahunty must state whose well-being counts and why, while Baggett must show that principled expansion remains unavailable or insufficient rather than merely absent from the abbreviated formulation. Locked score: The very strong band reflects precise counterexample construction, direct burden contact, careful conditional phrasing, and broad moral relevance, while recognizing the secular account's straightforward possibility of scope enlargement.

sections.title: Comparative Worldview Fit and Theistic Liabilities

pro.words: Theistic ethics requires a morally perfect, maximally great God, and moral considerations may narrow the field beyond arbitrary or capricious deities.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett rejects indiscriminate deity concepts and identifies moral perfection and maximal greatness as candidate constraints, directly answering the concern that unrestricted supernatural hypotheses explain everything equally. Principal limitation: The particular omni-properties and moral criteria remain underdeveloped, and using moral knowledge to identify morality's divine foundation risks circularity unless independent support distinguishes the candidate. Live burden: The affirmative must explain reliable identification, evidential access, and genuine discriminatory consequences, not merely describe the morally ideal being that would best fit the desired conclusion. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects substantive candidate restriction, direct engagement, appropriate qualification, and central relevance, while retaining significant reservations about specification, independent warrant, and unresolved access.

con.words: Methodological naturalism permits demonstrated supernatural causes but excludes unexplained divine labels that add no discriminating prediction or explanatory power.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty clearly distinguishes methodological from philosophical naturalism and conditionally permits supernatural explanation, thereby avoiding an a priori exclusion while demanding evidentially discriminating content. Principal limitation: The term demonstrable may impose a stronger admission standard than comparative abduction requires, since explanatory hypotheses can receive provisional support without experimental demonstration or deductive confirmation. Live burden: The objection must articulate an appropriately abductive evidential threshold, while Baggett must show that classical theism contributes testable differentiation, explanatory constraints, or independent access beyond renaming unresolved mystery. Locked score: The very strong band reflects conceptual correction, diagnostic relevance, conditional openness, and coherent methodological pressure, while retaining measured concern that the proposed standard may exceed the debate's comparative method.

pro.words: Some divine hiddenness may serve relational priorities beyond producing bare existence-belief, since recognizing a person exists is not equivalent to relationship.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Baggett offers a relevant distinction between bare belief and relationship, presenting hiddenness as potentially connected to relational priorities rather than simply denying the opposing evidence. Principal limitation: Other priorities remain underspecified, and the analogy does not explain why reliable awareness and noncoercive moral clarification could not coexist with freely chosen relationship. Live burden: The reply must address preventable harm, proportionality, and access to moral requirements, showing why the particular degree of uncertainty advances relational goods more effectively than available alternatives. Locked score: The strong and competent band reflects appropriate possibility-level calibration, direct contact with one component of hiddenness, and conceptual relevance, while registering incomplete responsiveness, limited warrant, and insufficient engagement with clarification.

con.words: Harmful, persistent uncertainty is morally unexpected if a good creator could clarify consequential truth while apparently sufficient natural explanations mislead inquiry.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty turns hiddenness into a specifically moral explanatory liability, conditionally connecting divine goodness, human inquiry capacities, apparently sufficient natural explanations, consequential uncertainty, and preventable harm. Principal limitation: The inference remains defeasible because relational, developmental, freedom-related, or other goods might justify some hiddenness, although merely naming such possibilities does not explain their proportionality. Live burden: Theism must show why less coercive clarification could not reduce serious error while preserving relational goods, whereas the objection must substantiate the relevant harms and feasible alternatives. Locked score: The very strong band reflects precise conditional structure, powerful worldview-level relevance, careful calibration, and direct engagement with the loving-creator hypothesis, while appropriately leaving room for developed countervailing reasons.

strengths: Landed a disciplined comparative framework spanning moral facts, knowledge, transformation, and rationality.
Landed a notably modest conclusion that treats morality as contributory evidence within the total record.
Landed the categorical-versus-instrumental distinction and a concrete animal-welfare scope challenge.
Landed clear qualifications concerning ordinary secular improvement and the rejection of arbitrary deity concepts.

blunders.text: The case did not fully establish that complete transformation is an explanation-demanding datum or specify its success conditions.
The loving-creator account depended on contested categorical authority and remained comparatively underdeveloped.
The replies on divine identification and hiddenness did not resolve reliable access, preventable harm, or less coercive clarification.

strengths: Landed foundational challenges to explanandum status, divine candidacy, and the representativeness of the abductive candidate pool.
Landed secular mechanisms for ordinary transformation, conscience, convergence, and goal-relative assessment.
Landed the distinction between philosophical and methodological naturalism while allowing conditionally demonstrated supernatural causes.
Landed strong identification, access, and moral-hiddenness objections against the claimed theistic explanatory advantage.

blunders.text: The well-being account left its initial normative commitment, internal tradeoffs, and response to categorical obligation incompletely explained.
The empathy and convergence accounts explained causal origins and practical coherence more fully than objective truth or categorical authority.
The demonstrability language risked imposing a stronger evidential threshold than comparative abduction itself requires.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that a carefully bounded cumulative inference from categorical authority, basic moral knowledge, transformative aspiration, and rational fulfillment can modestly favor classical theism when compared against fully specified secular alternatives.
premises: At least some moral judgments present themselves not merely as efficient means toward chosen ends but as requirements applying even when compliance frustrates immediate self-interest.
A personal ground is explanatorily relevant only if moral perfection constrains that ground independently and if moral access includes publicly discussable defeaters and correction procedures.
Properly basic moral beliefs can supply provisional knowledge when they survive reflection, role reversal, factual correction, and comparison with coherent counterexamples.
Transformative aspiration contributes evidence only when defined as a stable orientation toward moral repair, not as an unsupported expectation of literal perfection.
Theistic support should increase only when one integrated account explains categorical authority, fallible knowledge, correction, and long-range hope more economically than combined secular accounts.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the moral evidence can provide limited comparative support for classical theism only if these access, specification, reliability, and candidate-pool conditions are independently met.

newArguments.title: Normative convergence under correction
newArguments.text: Convergence becomes more evidentially interesting when it persists after factual education, reciprocal role reversal, exposure to unfamiliar interests, and removal of self-serving distortions. Such convergence would not prove a divine source, but it could support the claim that moral cognition tracks constraints deeper than local preference. The theistic case could then ask whether a morally perfect personal ground explains both authority and corrigible access better than secular rivals, while remaining answerable to comparative evidence.

newArguments.title: Relational clarity compatibility test
newArguments.text: A relational account of hiddenness should predict enough noncoercive clarity for responsible moral agency while leaving relationship freely chosen. Theism therefore gains credibility only if it can explain a middle range between overwhelming manifestation and harmful ambiguity: accessible moral reasons, corrigible traditions, and opportunities for sincere response without compelled affection. This framework converts a vague appeal to divine priorities into a comparative prediction and acknowledges that persistent destructive confusion would count against the hypothesis.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that moral experience currently supports disciplined secular inquiry more strongly than a theistic inference because natural mechanisms explain substantial phenomena while divine candidacy, access, discrimination, and hiddenness remain unresolved.
premises: Ordinary moral change, conscience, and substantial ethical convergence have plausible natural pathways through learning, empathy, reciprocal reasoning, institutions, and shared creaturely vulnerability.
Goal-relative assessment can be objective after foundational commitments are stated, although the commitments themselves remain open to public criticism, expansion, and revision.
A supernatural candidate should be admitted to comparison when it has discriminating content and evidential consequences, without requiring deductive proof or experimental reproduction.
Divine grounding supplies limited epistemic benefit unless people can identify the relevant deity, distinguish genuine requirements from projection, and correct harmful interpretive errors.
Comparative confidence should remain modest whenever multiple secular mechanisms can operate jointly and the broader candidate pool has not been representatively developed.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the available moral phenomena warrant continued secular explanation and methodological caution, while withholding a positive theistic inference unless candidacy, access, and comparative discrimination improve.

newArguments.title: Error-correction advantage
newArguments.text: An explanatory framework should be evaluated partly by its procedures for detecting and correcting moral error. Secular inquiry can compare outcomes, expose affected parties' testimony, revise institutions, and test whether principles survive reciprocal scrutiny. These procedures are imperfect, but their failures are publicly inspectable. A divine-command interpretation adds value only if it improves correction rather than multiplying disputed authorities. This criterion shifts comparison from the mere existence of moral convictions toward the reliability of practices that revise them.

newArguments.title: Explanatory decomposition
newArguments.text: The four moral phenomena need not share one ultimate explanation. Authority judgments, knowledge, transformation, and rational motivation may arise from partially independent social, cognitive, biological, and philosophical processes. A single theistic hypothesis gains no automatic economy merely by labeling all four effects together; it must outperform a decomposed secular model on fit, constraints, and error prediction. This approach also prevents failure in one secular mechanism from being treated as evidence that every component requires the same supernatural source.
